Martyn, Nichola




We need to consider these. It's not clear what the below means - 





what working arrangement is to be signed off?

what does solely working on common costs mean? For example, Pri and quantum: what is common costs on that? How would that work with Sarah? 

Does PG related matters mean all non-ALGLO work? For example, would it mean Michael ceasing to work on Volvo and Matt on FCA?

That last point clearly cannot work in terms of timings as they well know.





What in fact is being proposed - it is entirely not clear to me.




I'm not sure this does sound reasonable. I need to catch up with Alicia before we can confirm anything to the counsel team.




Thanks

Anna
​​​​Anna VargaPartner+44 (0) 7890 043 699

From: Martyn Day <mday@leighday.co.uk>
Sent: Wednesday, October 1, 2025 2:33 PM

CAUTION: This email originated from outside of the organization. Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe.

Counsel have asked us whether we are able to say to the court, through them, that we are satisfied the PG Case Leads will remain involved in the case until the end of the
 year.
Nic and I took the liberty to speak to them at lunchtime. They say they confirm they are happy to give that reassurance if the following conditions are met:-

that a working agreement is put in place to be signed off by you and us applying to the five of them, ie Michael Burke, Priyanka Gladson,
 Matt Hunt, Georgie Fallows, and Sarah Bingham - not to the wider PG NOx team;that for the remainder of their tenure at PG, the five of them solely work on common cost matters across the Pan NOx Litigations;that they are not responsible for conducting PG only related work;
that PG will update their various Claimant Committees that the case leads have stepped down and who the new case leads are within a
 reasonable time frame and in any event no more than 14 days;
That all sounds reasonable, so can you confirm you are content with this so we can give the assurance to the court.
Thanks
 
Martyn
 

















Martyn Day

{"emailHash":"0e7b078f628eacae4d57ecbd6421e2304db6f33ed0c2b7f20230e9c32d9c1083","parentHash":null,"sequentialName":"Email 2747","from":"Matt Hunt","to":"Raminder Grewal","subject":"Re: Formal grievance","date":"2025-11-14T19:21:59.117Z","attachments":true,"body":"


 P {margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;} 



Dear Raminder,




I am going to some time to consider your email, which is particularly demotivating to receive on the eve of the PCD section of trial.




Matt


From: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Friday, November 14, 2025 17:25
To: Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: Formal grievance
 



Dear Matt,




Thank you for attending the grievance meeting on 7 November 2025 and for setting out your concerns in writing. Georgina Fallows accompanied you to the meeting. 




I appreciate the demands of the ongoing PDD Trial and your willingness to engage in this process despite those pressures. My email confirms the outcome of the grievance process. 




1. Summary of Your Grievance

  Your grievance raised the following main issues:


Stress and adverse health effects, which you attribute to actions or omissions of senior leadership following the case leads’ resignations

Perceived lack of acknowledgement or response to you and colleagues regarding various concerns raised in emails

Conduct during the case-leads meeting on 24 October 2025, specifically a comment made by Anna Varga, Lead Emissions partner,  about the potential move of staff to JLG

Broader concerns about senior leadership, culture, media activity, and the leak of the interim report, which you indicated contributed to embarrassment, stress and concerns about the firm’s governance

A request for remedies to include an acknowledgement of stress caused by the firm, an apology and compensation

A request to leave immediately after the conclusion of the PCD phase of the trial (28 November 2025), rather than complete your contractual notice period ending 15 December 2025.





2. Findings




2.1 Responses to concerns raised by case leads

You expressed frustration that your emails and those of colleagues did not receive the responses you expected. Having reviewed the relevant correspondence, I acknowledge that some responses were delayed or brief. Responses were provided on a number of occasions,
 although they did not always address every point raised in depth. It is clear that senior leadership have been operating under significant time pressure during an exceptionally active phase of litigation, which affected the level of detail they were able to
 provide. Having reviewed the correspondence, I have found no evidence that any delays or brevity in replies were intended to ignore or dismiss your concerns.




2.2 Stress and adverse health effects

You described experiencing stress and having sought advice from a mental health nurse, who recommended self-certification. You explained that you continued working due to your commitment to the trial and clients.

The firm does take well-being seriously and your comment on the impact on you is noted. I have found no evidence that the firm engaged in conduct intended to cause you stress. The pressures you described appear to arise primarily from the ongoing challenges
 we face with our litigation and the organisational changes underway. While I recognise that you personally experienced stress, I have not found evidence of unreasonable treatment or any breach of duty by the firm. Whilst you confirmed in our meeting that you
 did not require any personal adjustments, you remain encouraged to use all available wellbeing resources, including visiting your doctor as advised by the medical nurse, as well as the employee assistance programme and your private medical insurance. If you
 wish to discuss any additional support we can offer you, I remain available to assist you.




2.3 The 24 October meeting
You raised concerns regarding a comment made by Anna Varga, which you felt was factually wrong and unhelpful. In reviewing this matter,  my view is that the comment was made without the intention you inferred; however,
 I do fully accept that it did not reflect the facts, as it is correct that not all staff leaving the firm are moving to JLG and you are right to point this out. 



2.4 Concerns regarding senior leadership, public communications, governance matters and
disclosure of the interim report

You raised several concerns relating to the wider conduct of senior leadership, including:


Embarrassment caused by public statements or media exchanges involving the firm 

Alleged tensions or disputes between senior individuals

The governance structure of the firm and its alignment with litigation strategy

The leak of an interim report to the media.





I fully acknowledge that these issues have caused you concern and that you perceive them as contributing to the pressures you have experienced and I also recognise that they may have affected the broader working environment for both you and your colleagues.
 However, after careful consideration, I must confirm that these matters relate to organisational governance, strategic communications and the conduct of senior individuals in their executive capacities and therefore do not relate specifically to your individual
 employment relationship or fall within the scope of the grievance procedure. In addition, several of the concerns you raised, particularly regarding the interim report leak and media activity, are already being considered through separate internal processes
 and cannot be managed through the grievance route. While I recognise that you understandably have strong views about these issues and feel they contributed to the stress you experienced, the evidence available does not indicate that they resulted in targeted
 or unreasonable treatment towards you as an individual.




3. Remedy

You requested an acknowledgement that the firm caused you stress, an apology, and compensation. After considering all of the information available, I do not find that the firm’s actions constituted unreasonable treatment, misconduct, or a breach of duty. Accordingly,
 I cannot conclude that the firm was responsible for causing the stress you describe and an apology would therefore not be appropriate in circumstances where the grievance has not been upheld. For the same reason, compensation is not warranted. That said, I
 recognise the pressures you have been under and am sorry that you have experienced this period as distressing. Although this does not amount to an acceptance of fault, I do want to acknowledge the impact you described during our meeting.




4. Request to Leave After the PCD Phase

To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>
Cc: Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: Notice of Resignation 

 




Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure
 you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm
 on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such,
 I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into
 the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim
 back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the
 employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm
 has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts
 on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into
 hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover
 the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael

Hi Anna,




Following on from yesterday and the calls with LD, a few things we would suggest are raised with Martyn. Firstly, it is important to say the Case Leads and PG team are wildly committed to this trial. That should not be in question.
 However, the AA (the executed version of which the case leads were only sent at 9.22AM this morning), which has been referred to in Court documents and has been incepted without the consent of those persons it applies to (either expressly in the case of the
 Case Leads or, as far as the wider team is concerned, by implication), causes concern. Additionally, the case leads have also raised serious concerns about the staff's  mental health that are yet to be addressed by the firm.




The AA was incepted with little to no visibility or consideration for how it will practically work (as is clear given Martyn's explanation in ​the call on 8 October was substantially different to our understanding of what it means,
 a view which we consider you, also on that call, shared). We need further clarity on the AA. This is true for both for the Case Leads, and the PG staff who will be indirectly subject to it - by way of taking instructions from the Case Leads who are under the
 supervision of Leigh Day.  As we have already told you, there is a real risk of the substantive PG team being entirely alienated by this agreement. These concerns were evidently ignored (including our concerns over the mental health and well-being of the staff)
 given it was executed without further recourse to us.  It also remains unclear what, if any, interaction LD is to have with the wider PG team, if they are not subject to the AA (and therefore direction and supervision), and whether, given this, the PG team
 would need to revert to one of the Case Leads for every interaction, instruction, discussion had with the LD team. An obvious example of this is the trial bundle/logistics workstreams which have largely been left between the excellent PG associates and LD
 with limited input from the case leads. It is fair to say the PG team carries that workstream and LD are unprepared to take it on. Similarly with Opus and issues at this morning's hearing. 




It would be helpful for an explanation, and for the physical AA, to be sent out to the wider PG team along with some practical guidance about what it means. It would be inappropriate for the Case Leads to do this given: i) we
 haven’t agreed to the AA; and ii) it has been incepted against our consent.




It would be helpful if the explanation covered:





what LD expect from the PG team  - do they simply expect the PG teams to "do what they're told, when they're told", or is there still going to be a collaborative
 approach (the former seems more likely given how things have happened over the last few days); 


how the "do what they're told, when they're told" works - or, indeed wider interaction works, in circumstances where the team isn't caught by the agreement. Will they need to take each instruction and run it past a Case Lead?

what happens in circumstances where the PG teams disagree with LDs position on decisions? How does this get resolved between the firms? We stress this is not a hypothetical. Aside from wider case strategy
 we have had immediate differences in opinion last week in terms of costs, with decisions being made and taken without reference to PG. This impacts all claimants, and, of course PG's clients. Further, in terms of wider points, as we have pointed out, LD do
 not have clients on some of the secondary or ALGLO cases, all of which are bound by the PDD trial judgment. It is easy to anticipate a diversion of opinion/strategy as the PDD trial develops which could impact PG only cases/clients and for which, under the
 AA the Case Leads cannot wear two hats.  

how working practices are going to change, both outwardly to the Ds and Court etc, and whether a working group should be set up to standardise approach e.g. do all things on the PG SharePoint move across
 to LD - what is the timeframe, how is it co-ordinated? Whilst an administrative concern this does have significance in terms of sheer volume and also maintaining/transferring admin rights for links particularly where the Defendants and the Court already retain
 access. 

How does it work for the costs team? 





Each of these, along with sight of the AA, will go some way to helping the PG staff understand the agreement they are now working under and hopefully to stop the wheels from falling off. This will also assist in answering questions

the advice from BWKC or any other counsel on the AA. This is especially true where many of the concerns we have raised overlap with those in the HSFK letter - including the regulatory position for us
 as lawyers, and the position on client consent. We still have not consented to the AA and we all have significant regulatory concerns. In particular we have not seen any advice which contradicts our position that client consent is necessary for the AA.

 make a decision, do the PG bods have to in turn report these to the Board / AV? Do we have to report where decisions have been made that we do not agree with? What is our internal reporting matrix for issues such as this? 

Will our COLP, in their role as COLP, be giving us sign off on the agreement, in addition to the Counsel advice?

As our COLP is now also a case lead (for Pan NOx and it appears individual cases), is there a delineation of the COLP roles, from the role of case lead,
 and CEO of the firm? How is this safeguarded?





If these questions are not answered to a satisfactory standard, then our regulatory concerns will remain and as regulated persons, we will need to consider our positions and what, if any, further steps we need to take.

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL

Dear all,

Thank you for your kind responses to my email last week. I write with a further update
to the Ford NOx Emissions Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally (the “Litigation”):

Role as Lead Solicitors  

 

Pogust Goodhead, the firm, has applied to step away from its role as "Lead Solicitor" in the Lead Case and Additional Lead Cases which are proceeding to the PDD Trial, on a temporary basis only. This application was partly heard at the PTR yesterday but the
 Court has not yet confirmed in it in an Order. Set out below is information on: i) what the role of Lead Solicitor is; ii) the reasons why the firm believes this step is necessary, including the advice of counsel; and iii) what this will mean for the firm,
 and the Ford Litigation as well as the PDD Trial. 

 

The firm must advise you that this step has not been taken due to the merits of the Litigation changing. We remain confident in the strength of the case and are confident in a successful conclusion.  The firm stepping down does not affect the substantive work
 it is doing for the Ford Litigation and PDD Trial. 

 

The intention to step down temporarily as Lead Solicitors is in the Lead Cases only, in fact, to ensure the cases are protected and the PDD Trial proceeds without disruption.  

 



What is the role of Lead Solicitor? 


  

The role of Lead Solicitor is a Court-appointed role. Currently, Pogust Goodhead and Leigh Day are appointed as joint Lead Solicitors for this Litigation. The role of Lead Solicitors formally entitles the firm, jointly with Leigh Day, to manage the Litigation
 on behalf of all Claimants, not just those who formally instruct this firm.  The role of Lead Solicitor is set out in paragraph 10 of the Ford Group Litigation Order.  

 

Pogust Goodhead are intending to step down temporarily as Lead Solicitor in the Lead Cases only, and Leigh Day will remain the sole Lead Solicitor for the Litigation during the course of the PDD Trial. Pogust Goodhead will remain Lead Solicitors in respect
 of the remaining Non-Lead Cases. Pogust Goodhead regaining their position as Lead Solicitors will be subject to Court approval.  

 



Why does the firm believe it needs to step down as Lead Solicitor for the purposes of the PDD Trial? 


 

The firm's decision arises following recent reports in the press regarding the firm, including internal management changes (including my resignation). While Pogust Goodhead is confident that recent changes will strengthen the firm and its governance structures,
 and that questions regarding ancillary matters do not raise any concerns as to the firm’s ability to conduct the litigation, the firm intends to step down temporarily in order to ensure that those reports, and the resulting attempts by the Defendants to exploit
 them, do not distract from the upcoming PDD Trial and derail the procedural timetable in any way, and ensure that we stay fully focused on the substantive issues for trial. This proposal is supported by the co-Lead Solicitors, the Steering Committees in the
 Lead and Non-Lead cases and Leading Counsel. Pogust Goodhead has, together with those external parties, determined that this course is best designed to further your interests and those of the Claimants as a whole 

 

We are available to discuss any questions you may have. If you would like a meeting to discuss this issue, we are of course happy to arrange a meeting with the appropriate people within the firm. 

 



What does this mean for the Ford Litigation and the PDD Trial 


 

Pogust Goodhead do not intend for this step to do anything other than bolster the strength of your position in the Litigation. Pogust Goodhead intends to continue working on this case under the authorisation and delegation of Leigh Day, with whom we
 have been working closely for years/the Steering Committee, of which we remain a key part, and will provide support through trial.  

 

The firm remains confident of achieving a successful outcome. 




Should you have any questions regarding the contents of this letter, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Yours faithfully,

Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>
Sent: Friday, September 26, 2025 4:52 PM
To: Richard Hayes <rhayes47@btinternet.com>; 'tobyh45@gmail.com' <tobyh45@gmail.com>; dinahlogan@hotmail.com <dinahlogan@hotmail.com>
Cc: Ford Litigation Team <fordteam@pogustgoodhead.com>
Subject: Re: CFO01: Ford Client Committee - Strictly Private and Confidential




STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL

Dear all,

I hope you are all well. I write further to my last update on 5 August 2025, to provide you with a brief update on the following matters as they relate to the Ford NOx Emissions Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally
 (the “Litigation”):


PDD Trial Preparation;
Claimants Mechanical Expert;
Quantum Trial and discontinuance;
Change in personnel.

PDD Trial Preparation and final Pre-Trial Review

We are fast approaching the commencement of the PDD Trial, with the first day of trial listed for 13 October 2025, and the trial due to run until 19 December 2025.

Our skeleton argument was filed and served on 19 September, representing a mammoth undertaking by the entire Solicitor team and the barristers. The Ford specific annex to the skeleton argument was filed and served on 24 September. There was a slight extension
 to the Ford annex on account of the Defendants providing a very late second witness statement from a Ford employee. While we were not obliged to permit this into evidence, we took the view after considering it, that the statement was in fact more helpful for
 us and the case to allow its entry, rather than refusing permissions. As a caveat to our permittance of its inclusion, we agreed a short extension to the Ford annex.

As soon as I am in a position to provide you with a copy of the skeleton argument (with redactions for confidential information) I will send this to you. I would hope this will be later this week. I am extremely pleased with the final version of the skeleton
 argument. Our counsel team have done a remarkable job and it presents the best possible case for the court to consider.

While negotiations on the final timetable continue between the parties, we are close to concluding the timetable.

The first week of trial, due to commence on 13 October 2025, will consist of the Claimants and the Defendants making their opening remarks to the Court, in essence setting the scene, before we then move into evidence on what constitutes Normal Driving Conditions
 and then turning to each individual manufacturer. The order of the manufacturers will be Mercedes, Ford, Peugeot Citroen, Renault and Nissan.

It is expected that the Ford evidence, including the cross examination of experts and witnesses, will start on or around 13 November and run for just over a week.

If any of you are interested in attending Court for any part of the trial, please let us know and we will be able to arrange this with you.

There is due to be a final “Pre-Trial Review” hearing before the Court on 6 October which we are preparing for and this hearing will aim to settle any final issues or disputes that may impact the smooth running of the trial. The parties are in the process of
 agreeing an agenda for this hearing, and we will provide you with a further update on this in due course.

Claimants’ Software and Mechanical Experts

As per my previous update, I confirmed that in a hearing on 10 September, the Court unfortunately did not side with the Claimants in respect of the expert applications, and gave some strict directions with regard to steps the parties were required to take in
 respect of the software evidence that had been prepared.

We have been working hard to prepare and finalise the software report with the redactions / removals as advised by the Court and a version of these amended reports was provided to the Defendants on 24 September. We are awaiting the Defendants’ response to this
 draft report.  

In respect of the Claimants' mechanical expert, the Claimants' barrister team have provided a note to us in which they have flagged certain concerns with the mechanical expert. They have raised that they are concerned how the expert will perform at trial and
 that certain precautions need to be taken with the expert. Importantly, however, they have not told us that these concerns impact on the prospects of success of the case and we remain confident in the case we have prepared against Ford.

 protestations from the Defendants, we have successfully implemented a Pan-Lead CRO, which has been constructed to assist in the sharing of confidential information across the cases. While this is helpful in permitted us to see documents from other cases, it
 does not alleviate the issue of transferring documents into the Pan-Lead CRO (as the Defendants continue to raise various issues regarding this) and it does not prevent those documents being confidential and only certain people being able to see them. This
 does not go to the principle of open justice, whereby the public should know the conduct of these manufacturers. It is and always has been our intention to seek to de-designate these documents so that they can be referred to openly and in public.

The DDH is shaped at doing precisely that; bringing those documents into the public and also to make the process of hearing these cases in court more feasible. Under present circumstances, any time a party wishes to discuss any documentation that is confidential,
 it would require the Court room to be emptied of people who are not within the CROs, which is simply unworkable. The DDH is intended to allow open justice to be carried out.

We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns, nor does it even mention them. We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical workstreams.  Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements. You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. On the points in your email: Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged” within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding that the new arrangement is entirely novel.   You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects:  a. Formal separation of supervision and control The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations.  b. Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer.  The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will not practically change much day to day.”   Tension with Employment Contracts Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract:  a. Duty of obedience and supervision Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract.  b. Regulatory oversight The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?   These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.   c. Consent and legal clarity The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer, yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise.  Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here.  This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly, whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA.  This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure.  We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue.  Client Consent If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can.  You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these circumstances. Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed you of our plans post-PG.   You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel – as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting this afternoon.” In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution.  You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common work?  We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those issues and how they can be addressed, such that we can move forward, together.   The Case Leads Michael Burke, Priyanka Gladson, Matthew Hunt, Sarah Bingham & Georgina Fallows ​​​​Sarah BinghamLegal Director+44 (0) 7484 085 187From: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Saturday, October 04, 2025 14:12To: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>; 60% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



60% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and

50% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;

Hi PG team, 
 
Further to the con with counsel on 13 November 2025 (note attached), we have drafted a letter to go to the Defendants on the points as advised by counsel.

 
Please can you review and provide any comments/amends. We think it would be sensible to run the draft past Simon T before it goes too.

 
By way of reminder, the key points to be made were:

 
1. Upcoming CMC and Budgeting Exercise
The first point should note the forthcoming CMC in January 2026 (referring to paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment) and raise for discussion the scope and form of any further budgeting exercise that may
 be required. It would be helpful to clarify whether there are any applicable deadlines for updating one or both of the T3 Expert Reports or the ADR/Settlement Discussions phase, including how to treat the incurred costs of the T3 Expert Reports.
 
2. Proposed Dates
The second section should explore the floating of potential dates. At this stage, it is recognised that the time required will depend upon the Court’s decision regarding the scope of any further budgeting.
 Nonetheless, it may be constructive to propose an initial exploration of possible dates for a hearing, anticipated to require no more than one day. Dates to avoid will need to be gathered for the entire cost counsel team on both sides, before writing to check
 the Court's availability, including that of Senior Cost Judge Rowley. We propose that the hearing be listed before the end of April, as this would enable the ADR phase to be accommodated prior to the commencement of the Second General Budget.
 
3. ADR Phase and Budgeting Assumptions
The third section should concern the ADR/Settlement Discussions phase. With reference to the relevant paragraphs of the CMH2 judgment, the key issue preventing completion of the budgeting for this phase
 has been the divergence between the parties’ underlying assumptions and expectations. It would therefore be appropriate to invite the Defendants to indicate whether they have any proposals to align or harmonise the assumptions upon which the respective budgets
 are based.
 
Many thanks,
Sophia

Morning Sarah,
 
Ahead of our call to discuss at 11:30am, I just thought I’d flag some initial thoughts on the below, which we can then discuss later.
 
Wording of draft Order
Happy to discuss later this morning, but from my perspective, I’m not too concerned by Ds’ drafting of para 3.
For Experts, it seems to me inevitable that the court will want to budget them once the question of disciplines is resolved (and will want to whatever the wording of the order).
For ADR, wouldn’t it be in the Claimants’ favour
not to budget (given the scale of our estimates, and the likely approach which the court would take to them), if the court had any inclination not to do so? If so, don’t we want to give room for the court to decide that ADR is actually too difficult/uncertain
 to budget at the moment, rather than say they are forced to do so?
If that’s right, I would be inclined to go with Ds’ version of paragraph 3. But happy to discuss on our call.
 
CMH2 Consequentials
This has reminded me – have we had a decision on the CMH costs order yet?
 
Timing of CMH3 (Or CMH2.2, however we want to think of it!)
I agree that if there is to be further budgeting post-January we will need to crack on with it, there’s no point trying to drag our heels.
However, query whether a Feb CMH is a bit ambitious. Presumably we need time, post Jan CMC to:

Collect estimates based on decisions made, and update the 2x phases – min 10 days?Time for updates Prec Rs, in both directions – min 7 days?Gap to a hearing – c.7-10 days?
I can see that it wouldn’t be ideal to have the CMH in March, but I can see it happening as a matter of practicality, and it shouldn’t be the end of the world. It would be a fairly
 short and straightforward hearing.
I also doubt that it will really be possible to know exactly how much time will be required until at the Jan 26 CMC and hearing what the judges are deciding needs to be done.
Again, if the impracticalities end up pushing the court away from budgeting (at least in respect of ADR, which is likely to be harder than Experts), is that necessarily a bad thing?
(Also, surely the ADR costs wouldn’t start being incurred until end of April 2026, given they are in Second General?)
 
Whether costs counsel need to attend at the Jan CMC (22-23 Jan 2026)
Unfortunately(?) I am in Mexico from 17-31 Jan, but I will ask the clerks re Ben and Theo.
 
Budgeting framework
Unless it’s something the Ds are keen on, I’d be minded to just keep this as simple as possible. I don’t think this is a variation because there has been no budget set for Experts/ADR
 as phases.
I think the starting point, and probably the simplest answer, is that there would be two fresh phases for Experts and ADR with ‘incurred’ costs running (in the way we have done it
 previously) to the date of CMH3 – save that, for ADR, so long as the hearing was before the end of April, that would actually remain unchanged.
Once set, the ADR phase could be added to an updated Second General quite easily, as the incurred date is likely to be unaffected.
But even for the Experts, I don’t see why that couldn’t be added to the same document as the other T3 phases, once set. It would have a different ‘incurred’ cut off date, but everyone
 would know that (the relevant order would make it clear) and we could add a footnote to the face of the budget for the avoidance of doubt.
Overall, my view is we should (a) keep it simple, and (b) seek to agree our proposed approach with Ds in advance, much like we did on incurred dates previously. I don’t think we
 should decide our approach without knowing what their thoughts on it are.
 
Preparation for Budgeting
Let’s perhaps discuss this on the call.
It seems like there might be some discussions which can be had in advance of the Jan CMC in relation to different foreseeable scenarios to get the ball rolling on information gathering.
 But my first reaction is that these various potential changes, and the likelihood we won’t know which applies until 23 Jan, is why a February 2026 seems a little ambitious to me.
 
Other variations to T2/First General Budgets
I suppose it will depend on what the details of the envisaged variations are, but I am sceptical about whether the court will have any appetite for engaging in questions of variations
 to the T2/G1 budgets at this stage. Surely the costs will all have been incurred by the time any such variation hearing comes to be held (and perhaps even before we make an application)?
If that’s right, the court will surely say that these are questions to be dealt with on the basis of whether there is a ‘good reason to depart’ on assessment, rather than a variation
 (which is intended to be a largely prospective process). See Persimmon Homes Ltd & Anor v Osborne Clark & Anor
[2021] EWHC 831 (Ch), at [134]-[136].
And in any event, we would have to be conscious of the risk that:

The Ds use it as an opportunity to object and definitive close down any hope of recovering the additional costs (rather than leaving open the question of a ‘good reason to depart’);
 andDs might well say their costs have increased too, and seek their own increases to those budgets, with knock-on consequences for ATE levels etc.
 
Looking forward to discussing further at 11:30.
Thanks,
Simon

EXTERNAL EMAIL

Dear Ben, Theo and Simon,


We are writing in advance of the January 2026 CMC to flag the preparatory work required for the non-budgeted
 phases following CMH2.


Background and inconsistency in draft order
A CMC is listed for 22-23 January 2026 to consider further disclosure, expert disciplines, testing of post-update
 characteristics and other such matters that are confirmed as issues for the CMC by the court.
 
The CMH2 judgment states at paragraph 124:

“The question of expert evidence is to be considered at the CMC in January 2026 and it is plainly the case that there is a fundamental dispute as to whether there should
 be the expert evidence currently contemplated. In particular, the unusual specialism of consumer behaviour is challenged and we were not entirely clear from the explanations of counsel as to the utility of such evidence.  Since the extent of the expert evidence
 still needs to be determined, we think it would be better to budget that phase once the court has ruled further.”

Paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment concludes:



“We propose to re-consider the budgeting of this phase in January alongside the expert reports phase in the
 Tranche 3 budgets.”



The Defendants’ draft wording in the costs consequences order (not yet sealed), which we did not amend, currently
 states at paragraph 3:



“At the CMC listed in January 2026, the Court will consider whether there should be costs budgeting of
 the Expert Report phase of the parties’ Tranche 3 Budgets and/or the ADR phase of the parties’ Second General Budgets and, if so, give directions in that regard.”



The proposed draft wording departs from the judgment. The judgment proceeds on the basis that those phases
will be reconsidered for budgeting, whereas the draft order suggests only that the Court will consider whether there should be budgeting. What is clear is that budgeting for those phases (and potential "new" phases per the below) must occur, it
 is a question of when. 


Our proposal
We propose to write to the Defendants inviting amendment of paragraph 3 of the draft Order to reflect the
 judgment, namely, that the Court will reconsider budgeting of (i) the Expert Reports phases in Tranche 3 cost budgets; and (ii) the ADR phases in the Second General budgets. Further cost management directions will be provided at the January
 CMC. Although it would be advantageous to delay CMH3 if costs were to be deemed incurred until CMH3 (see option 2 below),  we believe that the best time for a potential CMH3 will be in February 2026. Any time after this will mean that a budgeting exercise
 is significantly less effective given a) March will not be a suitable time for this hearing to be listed as a result of the PDD Spring 2026 hearing which is listed for 3 weeks (a fourth in reserve) from 2 March 2026), and b) the phases that will be being considered
 in the cost budgeting will commence following the CMC in January and the costs of those phases will largely have been incurred before April 2026. We do, however, have a CMC listed in April 2026.  

Attendance at the January CMC
The question is whether attendance by costs counsel will be required at the January 2026 CMC. This will depend
 on whether further cost management directions can be agreed between the parties prior to the hearing. In any event, could you please confirm your availability for 22-23 January 2026, just in case.
 
Budgeting framework and incurred costs
As the Tranche 3 and Second General cost budgets have already been cost-managed, it may be considered that the T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases now fall within
 the PD3E §7.6 regime (variation to budgets).

We need to address how to present the T3 Expert Reports costs incurred between 17 July 2025 (the first day
 post-CMH2) and the listing of CMH3. There will be no incurred costs for the Second General ADR phase as it is not due to commence until 1 April 2026.


We suggest that the Lead Solicitors quantify those incurred costs in any event, but that:


·                    
Option 1: the “incurred to” date within the Cost Management Order remains 16 July 2025, with a note that £X has been incurred since that date and will form part of
 the estimated allowance; or


·                    
Option 2: a separate cut-off date (CMH3) is adopted for the T3 Expert Reports phase only.


Preparation for budgeting


T3 Expert Reports Phase


There will be an initial change to the estimated costs within the T3 Expert Reports phase following the January
 CMC:


·                    
Scenario A: including consumer-behaviour expert evidence (if permission is granted at the January CMC), i.e. the version presented at CMH2; and
·                    
Scenario B: excluding those costs (if permission is not granted).

Scenario C: revising consumer- expert evidence costs (if the Court confirms that permission remains for the consumer-behaviour expert but clarifies/limits
 the scope)


However, the potential impact on the T3 Expert Reports phase extends beyond the consumer-behaviour expert
 application. If permission is refused, it may still impact the scope of the remaining expert evidence and the division of work among those experts.


We also must consider whether, and if so how much, further expert evidence is required from the software and
 mechanical expert engineers, especially in relation to the characteristics of the vehicle and the impact of updates. 


In addition to the above, the Court will also be considering the potential application(s) concerning expert
 testing of vehicles for quantum at the January CMC. Our T3 Mercedes, Ford, Nissan-Renault and Citroen Peugeot assumptions all say the same within the T3 Expert Report phase: "No provision is made at this stage, and costs are not included for unilateral testing on
 non-Core Sample Vehicles or joint testing on the Core Sample Vehicles." Even if the Court determines the outcome of that application at the CMC, it is likely that the Court will direct the parties to agree the testing protocol thereafter (in a manner similar
 to the PDD process). The costs will need to mirror the protocol. If testing is ordered, in addition to the costs of testing (which may fall under a separate, additional phase),   the scope of the technical expert reports and therefore the costs of their reports
 may be impacted, as referenced above.


Lastly, the NALGLO defendants are able to make applications in January for permission to adduce their own
 expert evidence. This is an issue that was not originally budgeted for.


T3 Disclosure Phase


There is also an application for additional disclosure listed for the January CMC, which may require re-opening of
 that approved phase.


We would welcome views on CMH3 budget preparation.


Collateral Use / De-designation Workstream
There is also a separate collateral use / de-designation workstream, which was kept outside the scope of budgeting during PDD and to date, costs have been dealt
 with summarily. We would like to discuss with you whether it would now be in our interests for the quantum equivalent of that workstream to be included within cost budgeting at this stage. Depending on how that workstream evolves, there may be a case for including
 it within the Tranche 3 framework.

Future housekeeping – CMH1 budgets
Finally, as we review the other phases and CMH3 appears to be a final sweep-up, it may be sensible to consider
 revisiting the CMH1-approved budgets for PDD and the First General phases to determine whether any variations are now appropriate. We consider that significant variations may be required, and this may be an appropriate time to sweep up those proposed variations. 

Counsel’s advice sought

1.                  
Agreement that paragraph 3 of the draft order should be amended to mirror paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment.


2.                  
Whether the parties should write jointly to the Court or raise at the Fortnightly Meeting to confirm their intention to set further cost management directions at the January
 CMC.


3.                  
Whether costs counsel should attend at some point during the January CMC, given the likelihood of directions.


4.                  
Confirmation as to whether the T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases are properly presented under PD3E §7.6 regime (variation).


5.                  
Preferred approach to presenting costs incurred between 17 Jul 2025 and CMH3 for T3 Expert Reports.


6.                  
Whether the current T3 Expert Reports and 2G ADR phases should be updated (and on what basis), including in light of:


o       
(a) any refusal or grant of permission for the consumer-behaviour expert and/or change in the scope of the expert evidence for any of the expert disciplines;
(b) the application for additional disclosure; and
(c) the NALGLO applications for permission to adduce expert evidence.


7.                  
Guidance on how to deal with the vehicle testing application for quantum. Perhaps to be dealt with in a separate phase, if appropriate.


8.                  
Whether it is strategically advantageous for the quantum equivalent of the collateral use / de-designation workstream to be brought within budgeting at this stage.


9.                  
Whether the CMH1-approved budgets for PDD and the First General phases, should now be revisited under PD3E §7.6 to reflect significant developments since their approval.

Happy to discuss the above further in a meeting, if helpful.
 
Kind regards
Sarah

 CRO.

 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.

 statements for the January 2026 CMC.

{"emailHash":"d761807bd8f158838e2adbb686146d3d276121d5505e8900224fdafb2f7a5bdc","parentHash":null,"sequentialName":"Email 6053","from":"Greg Lewis","to":"R HAYES; Toby Hannam; Dinah Logan","subject":"Re: Re: CFO01: Ford Client Committee - Strictly Private and Confidential","date":"2025-12-09T08:24:04.000Z","attachments":true,"body":"
 P {margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;} 



STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL




Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,




I am writing to update you on progress towards the Quantum Trial scheduled for October 2026.






On 21 November, we filed and served Individual Particulars of Quantum ("IPQ"s) for 36 of the 40 Sample Claimants across the Pan-NOx litigation. The IPQs for the Ford Sample Claimants are attached for your reference. IPQs for the remaining
 four Sample Claimants will be filed and served on 17 December. Broadly, these IPQs:






Specify the causes of action being pursued by each Sample Claimant — for purposes of the Quantum Trial, the two causes of action being adjudicated are breach of statutory duty and (save in specific instances where time-barred) breach of contract; and


Set out particulars of the nature of each Sample Claimant's interest in the vehicle (eg, outright purchase, hire purchase, PCP, hire agreement), amounts paid, date of acquisition and disposal, etc.






On 17 December, we will be filing and serving supplements to the IPQs that either (i) specify the quantum of loss claimed in respect of these causes of action or (ii) state with particularity the steps required to particularise the loss (ie, via
 expert evidence). We have been liaising with expert advisors to determine a detailed approach to quantifying loss and are currently finalising that approach for purposes of the IPQ supplements.





On 22-23 January 2026, a first Quantum Case Management Conference ("CMC") will be held. The parties are to make applications for any matters they want determined at the CMC by 8 January 2026. The precise agenda for the CMC is not yet certain,
 but we expect to make applications on behalf of the Claimants for further disclosure from the Defendants and possibly to address other case management issues.





The remaining timetable to the Quantum Trial is very compressed, with a first tranche of disclosure to be served by the parties in March 2026, Defences to the IPQs to be served around the same time, witness statements and a second CMC in April 2026 and initial
 exchange of expert reports in May 2026.




We will keep you updated at regular intervals on progress and seek your instructions where appropriate. In the meantime, please do not hesitate to contact me with any questions or if you would like to discuss the case generally.

Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has

Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform
 to a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase
 their output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects
 certain Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge
 the LNT of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due
 to be heard next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues.

 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way.

Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation.

Dear all,




I hope you are well and are enjoying the half term break. 




I write in relation three matters, one of which we require your instructions in relation to:





an update on the second week of trial;

an application by the Ford Defendants to amend some of their pleadings -
we require your instructions in relation to this; and

the discontinuance of Mr Gormley (as previously discussed in my update of 26 September 2025.





Second and third week of trial




Week two of the PDD Trial focused on the issue of what are conditions which are “reasonably likely to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use” for the purposes of identifying prohibited defeat devices in the Defendants’ vehicles. The Court
 heard from experts in the field of what constitutes "normal driving" and climatology. For the Claimants, our experts were Professor Tate (normal driving) and Professor Mills (climatology) and for the Defendants, Professor Hausberger (normal driving) and Professor
 Chapman (climatology). 




Ultimately, while this was important evidence which will underpin the definition of "prohibited defeat device", as the Judge remarked at the end of the evidence - it would not be a central part of her ultimate judgment. 




That said, and as we have advised our insurers; we think that the Claimants’ evidence and cross-examination of the Defendants’ experts has clearly had a positive impact on the judge’s views of this element of the case. While we anticipate that the likely approach
 Lady Justice Cockerill will take is to set a limit on the range of conditions which would reasonably be encountered during normal vehicle operation and use, however, we do not expect that she will be inclined to adopt an excessively restrictive set of boundaries
 (which the Defendants have advocated for) in light of the Claimants’ case on this issue.




Starting tomorrow, Mercedes kicks us off into the manufacturer specific sections of the trial. Mercedes will run from tomorrow, 29 October 2025, until 6 November. Ford then starts on 10 November and runs until 18 November. Preparations for Ford are going well.
 As previously offered, if any of you wish to attend on the 10,11,12,13, 17 or 18 November, please let me know. You are most welcome to attend and we can arrange for this to happen. 




Defendants' application to amend




On Friday afternoon, we received correspondence from the Ford Defendants, proposing amendments to two of their Individual Defences. Their reason for this exceptionally late application, they have said, is that they have given "careful consideration to the
 fidelity of their pleadings in light of those [opening] submissions, and have taken the view that two of the IDEFS....out properly to be amended." The effect of these amendments is that they are seeking to change their case on a central point of dispute
 between the parties. As summarised by one of the Claimants legal team - these proposed amendments mean "at the very lease, their legal representatives (and their mechanical expert) were misled (though they would very likely say they were misinformed)". 




While we would be within our right to refuse these amendments, having taken advice from our counsel team, we are minded to permit the Defendants to have these amendments, on the proviso that they pay our costs on the indemnity basis. Costs on the indemnity
 basis in essence mean that becuase the conduct of the paying party has been unreasonable, the burden to prove that the costs claimed is less. In practical terms, it means that the costs recovered are generally higher than otherwise. Counsel have also
 advised that it is in our favour to permit this as it allows us to put under the Judge's nose that the Ds have in essence lied, or at least not been fully truthful, about the software in their vehicles. 




We have written to the Defendants to propose this, but ultimately we must also take your instructions on this. It is our advice that, in the event Ford agree to pay our wasted costs, we will consent to the application.
Can you please confirm by return that you instruct us to consent to the application?




Mr Gormley

Proceed to discontinue Mr Gormley’s claim in England & Wales; and
Remove Mr Gormley from the Ford Group Register.

We are in the process of doing so. We have liaised with the ATE  provider on this as there are, as advised, necessarily costs associated with this. The insurers have confirmed that they will cost the costs of this discontinuance, but reserve the right to seek

We will now proceed with the discontinuance of Mr Gormely's claim. No further action is required form you in respect of this.

I hope you're well.



I am writing regarding the Pan-NOx Emissions Litigation, specifically regarding the viability of securing additional LOI coverage through further excess layer insurance policies.



Following the handing down of the judgment (10th September 2025) after the Second Costs Management Hearing (15-16 July 2025), the Defendants have revisited their position on applications for security for costs. We
 have therefore undertaken a further review of the potential adverse costs resulting from the Tranche 3 Quantum Trial and the Second General Budget. 



Previously, our assessment of ATE sufficiency was calculated on the following basis:



60% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



60% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to Spring 2026.



Given the level of incurred costs and the criticisms between Defendants regarding their figures, we consider that the sufficiency calculation can be revised downwards without materially affecting the adequacy of coverage.
 We propose the following revised basis:



50% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



50% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to 31 July 2026.
